newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan says Uganda attacking from south.
newsitem.headline: Sudan says Uganda attacking from south.

text.p: Sudan has said that Uganda attacked two border towns in the south to support rebels fighting the Khartoum government.

State television interrupted its regular broadcast late on Sunday to read a statement from the armed forces saying that the rebels had launched their attacks from Uganda and Zairean areas under Ugandan influence.
"The bombing of Bazi was conducted from the Zairean towns of Ariwara and Ambakolo which are overrun by Tutsi rebels supported by Uganda," said the official statement.

It also said that the rebels, who launched a widescale offensive on the east and south in January, had attacked Kaya town on the Uganda border and were advancing on Yei, a key centre close to the Zaire border.
"The Ugandan forces at 5 a.m. (0300 GMT) on Sunday launched a heinous aggression on the Sudanese border town on Kaya from the Ugandan areas of Koboko and Keriwa," the statement said.
On Sunday, the rebel Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) said they had captured Kaya and that they were advancing on the man southern town of Juba.

"The SPLA forces launched a simultaneous attack on Kaya and the Yei-Juba road and captured Kaya town. Our forces are three kilometres (two miles) from Yei town. We will capture it at any time," SPLA spokesman Yassir Arman told Reuters in Eritrea.
The SPLA, led by John Garang, has been fighting the Khartoum government since 1983, demanding independence for the mainly Christian and animist south of the Sudan from the Moslem and Arabised north.
Kaya, west of the Nile, is only 30 km (20 miles) north of the Uganda border, and 70 km (44 miles) east of Yei.

Arman said the rebel forces had also attacked Morobo, and had captured Gumuni garrison on the Yei-Juba road. The headquarters of the National Tobacco Company near Gumuni was also in SPLA hands, he said.
The rebel claim was the first indication in several weeks of the progress of the offensive, in which the opposition captured two towns on the eastern Ethiopian border.

Sudan has accused neighbours Eritrea, Ethiopia and Uganda of fighting alongside the rebels, who want to pressure the Khartoum goverment and spark a popular uprising to topple the rule of Lieutentant-Genera Omar Hassan al-Bashir.

The three states deny any involvement but Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni threatened last month to resolve his problems with Sudan on the battlefield. Khartoum and Kampala accuse each other of sheltering rebels.

Sudanese goverment spokesman al-Tayeb Ibrahim Mohamad Khair told state television that the rebels were using large numbers of tanks and artillery "which indicated foreign involvement in the aggression".

Armed forces spokesman Mohamad Senoussia Ahmed also said that the attack was "the start of the implementation of recent threats to Sudan by the Ugandan president" and Khair added that Sudan maintained the right to repulse the attack.
